Commentary:
At Riverside College Ground in Eastport, Cedar Vale won the toss and took first use of a surface that looked friendly enough once a batter got in, yet not so flat that Ridgeport could simply wait for mistakes, and that small tension shaped the whole match because Cedar Vale were forced to keep rebuilding, keep answering pressure, and keep finding one more scoring phase whenever Ridgeport thought the innings had finally opened. Liam Hart was the spine of it from the first over to deep into the last ten, and the important thing about his innings was not just the size of it, it was the timing of each layer, because he began as the senior hand beside Noah Pierce, then became the repair batter after the first wicket, then the controller through the middle, and finally the accelerator once Mason Reed joined him with the game sitting in that dangerous area where one more wicket could have dragged the total back toward something merely good. Noah’s early hand was not noisy in a careless way; it was a proper opening role, leaving enough, taking the singles that were there, and still putting away the loose width often enough to make Ridgeport spread before they really wanted to. That first stand reached into the nineties before Noah was finally held off Arjun Nair, and although the scoreboard had a healthy look, Ridgeport were not out of the innings because they struck again soon after, Owen Vale going cheaply to Kabir Shah, and for a moment the rhythm changed from clean platform to a more watchful, slightly awkward middle-over rebuild. Liam did not let that awkwardness become panic. He had already made his first major contribution in the opening stand, then he added a small settling phase with Owen, then found a more durable partner in Riley Brooks, whose twenty-nine was the kind of support innings that looks modest until you notice where it arrived. Riley kept the bowlers from locking everything onto Liam, and the pair moved Cedar Vale past the stage where a double strike would have fully reset the innings. Ridgeport still found their best passage just after that. Kabir Shah, who was easily their sharpest pressure bowler through the middle, removed Riley, then pinned Evan Stone almost immediately, and suddenly Cedar Vale were four down with the score only just past the one-sixty mark. That was Ridgeport’s doorway. The captain was still there, clearly set, clearly dangerous, yet the fielding side had exposed the new batters and forced Cedar Vale to decide whether they were going to protect the innings or push it forward. Mason Reed’s arrival settled that question. He did not play like someone walking in to admire a captain’s hundred from the non-striker’s end; he attacked enough to move the field, rotated enough to keep Liam facing useful matchups, and kept Ridgeport from building a long dot-ball squeeze. The fifth-wicket partnership was the real hinge of the match, a stand just short of three figures, with Liam taking the innings from command into domination and Mason giving the innings its second active scoring line. Liam’s hundred, when it came, felt less like a single celebration and more like the result of several small battles already won: first the new ball, then the loss of partners, then the middle-over squeeze, then Kabir’s double intervention, and finally the need to turn a competitive total into one that would feel heavy before Ridgeport even began the chase. Vikram Rao eventually removed him for a superb one hundred and thirty-six, and that wicket gave Ridgeport a short emotional lift, yet the innings had already crossed its most important line. Mason stayed long enough to add a brisk fifty-eight, Caleb Finn gave the last overs a cleaner finish than Ridgeport wanted, and even the small late events mattered: Theo Blake going quickly, Jack Morrow being run out, Sam Cole watching the final scraps from the other end, Caleb stealing what he could from the closing balls. Cedar Vale reached three hundred and twelve for eight, and the score felt earned because it had been built through one large captain’s innings, one strong opening platform, one urgent repair period, one decisive fifth-wicket answer, and enough end-overs pressure to stop Ridgeport from claiming they had dragged things back. Ridgeport’s bowling card had moments without quite becoming a full innings of control. Kabir Shah’s three wickets gave them their best route into the contest, and Arjun Nair was tidy enough to deserve the opening breakthrough. Vikram Rao took the wicket everyone wanted, Dev Malik picked up late reward, and Rohan Mehta kept searching for changes, but the attack still leaked through too many separate channels. A few wides here, a heavy over there, a partnership that lasted one spell too long, and suddenly a chase that might have been uncomfortable became a chase that required a near-perfect top order. Ridgeport tried to meet that problem through Rohan Mehta’s intent. Their captain came out with the only realistic attitude: he could not block his way toward three hundred and thirteen, so he went at the new ball, drove firmly, pulled when Cedar Vale missed short, and gave the first few overs a feeling that this reply might at least have teeth. Ishan Bedi fell with the score still in the twenties, caught from Caleb Finn’s bowling, and Vikram Rao followed after a short, slightly cramped stay, Mason Reed hitting the stumps and removing one of the players Ridgeport needed to bat long. Even then, Rohan kept the innings breathing. He added enough with Kabir Shah to keep the rate from dying completely, and for a few overs Cedar Vale had to respect the shot-making rather than simply wait. The stumping changed that. Jack Morrow was sharp, Riley Brooks had drawn Rohan out of his crease, and once the captain was gone for thirty-nine, Ridgeport lost the one batter who had been making Cedar Vale adjust their lines rather than just execute their plan. Kabir and Arjun Nair then produced Ridgeport’s largest partnership of the chase, and that tells the story by itself because it was a useful stand, a sensible stand, even a necessary stand, yet it was not a stand that could seriously drag the target back into view. Kabir’s thirty-four gave the middle overs some structure, Arjun’s long stay gave them resistance, and the pair did stop a complete early collapse, but the scoring tempo was already too heavy. Sam Cole removed Kabir at just over a hundred, and from that point Ridgeport’s innings became a sequence of small attempts rather than one joined chase. Nikhil Suri came and went after a brief stay, Arjun kept occupying the crease without fully changing the pressure, Dev Malik gave Mason Reed a wicket after making a compact thirteen, and Cedar Vale’s fielders began to look more certain with every passing over. Aarav Sen gave the lower order its one lively pulse. He struck cleanly enough to force the deep field back for a while, and with Kian Oberoi and then Tariq Alam passing through quickly, his role shifted from rescue to resistance to simple damage control. The scoreboard briefly crept toward a more respectable shape, helped by extras and by Aarav’s willingness to swing when the ball was in his slot, yet Cedar Vale never looked properly threatened because wickets kept arriving before any one phase could become a partnership. Mason Reed’s three wickets were valuable because they cut through the lower-middle section, Riley Brooks took out the captain and later Arjun, which removed both early tempo and long resistance, and Sam Cole’s four wickets gave the finish a clean, decisive edge. Theo Blake’s wicketless spell still mattered because it closed off easy release overs, and Arun Wells, even without a wicket, helped Cedar Vale move into their bowling plan before the main pressure bowlers took over. Ridgeport were finally all out for one hundred and seventy-two in the forty-third over, Aarav the last to fall, and the margin of one hundred and forty runs matched the shape of the day. Cedar Vale were not simply better because they had one huge score from Liam Hart, although that was the obvious headline; they were better because every meaningful pressure point produced an answer. The opening stand gave them stability, the middle rebuilt after quick wickets, the fifth-wicket pair broke Ridgeport’s best chance, the tail-end scoring added punishment, and then the bowling group never allowed Ridgeport’s reply to link its fragments into a real chase. Liam Hart was therefore the correct player of the match: his one hundred and thirty-six was the innings that set the match’s terms, survived the only serious Ridgeport squeeze, and gave Cedar Vale enough weight on the board that even Ridgeport’s better passages felt temporary rather than threatening.

Seabrook won by two hundred and five runs, and the margin feels earned because the match was not decided by one sudden collapse alone; it was built through sustained batting control first, then confirmed by a chase that never developed a coherent shape.
